description: This case study is a Congressional Research Service report, RL33124, on how Hurricanes Katrina and Rita disrupted US oil and gas supply in autumn 2005, in the version updated on 6 April 2006 (an earlier version dated 21 October 2005 is also listed). The summary states that the storms shut down offshore production that supplies 25% of US crude oil and 20% of natural gas, along with refineries in Louisiana, Alabama, Texas and nearby states, about 1.3 million barrels per day or 8% of national refining capability. Sections cover crude oil production, imports and transportation, refineries and product pipelines, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, the coordinated International Energy Agency release, inventories and prices, relaxation of motor fuel standards, natural gas pipelines and processing, gas prices and inventories, and electric power. Access: free HTML and PDF from the EveryCRSReport archive; no licence is stated on the page. Coverage is the US Gulf Coast supply chain. Caveats: only the summary and contents were read here, and the report is dated 2006, so it predates later recovery figures. It suits resilience and cascading failure studies of fuel supply chains, and no directly related records are catalogued yet.

name: Oil and Gas Disruption From Hurricanes Katrina and Rita (CRS report RL33124, updated April 2006)
outcomes: The two storms shut down Outer Continental Shelf oil and gas production, the source of about 25% of US crude oil and 20% of natural gas output, and about 1.3 million barrels per day of refining capacity, roughly 8% of national capability. Imports and a coordinated International Energy Agency stock release covered part of the refined product shortfall; 30 million barrels were made available from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and only 11 million barrels were sold. About 3% of US gas consumption was still shut in when the report was updated in April 2006.
